utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. First of all, my apologies, not on behalf of the Chamber but on my own behalf, for the late start. I apparently had not properly assessed the time I needed for other things I was busy with. Apologies for that. Preliminaries, I've got one, but I was informed that both the Prosecution and the Simatovic Defence had a matter to be raised. Mr. Groome -- Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. We have two brief submissions I'd like to make in private session with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dimitrijevic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, first of all, our apologies that you had to wait for a while. We had to deal with a few other urgent matters. You'll now be examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Dimitrijevic. Would you be so kind as to tell me your full name.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Jovan Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of January --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the year. Could the witness please repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What are you by profession, Mr. Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dimitrijevic, the interpreters could not hear the -- your year of birth. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, you said that you graduated in economy. After you completed your studies in economy, did you find employment? And when, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I found employment in 1980 in a company in Slovenia. It had a branch in Belgrade. The name of the company was Krka and it was from Novo Mesto.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I currently work as an official in the Football Association of Serbia, and I have full-time employment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Up until when and where did you work in the Krka company, which had its headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked there until 1991, until the beginning of 1991. First of all, initially, I worked in the commercial department; and after three years, I was a representative of the headquarters and -- or I was a deputy director -- or, rather, an acting director and then I became the director of that branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Why did you stop working in the Krka company?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Given the events in Yugoslavia at the time, there was the beginning of the war and the beginning -- there was the beginning of the war in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and Slovenia seceded from Yugoslavia; and as a result, I was not only dismissed but everyone else was affected, everyone else working for that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you at some point in time in 1991 report as a volunteer? And where and when, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I reported as a volunteer towards the end of November in the military section of the municipality, which is the Palilula municipality in Belgrade. That's my municipality. But given my years, as I was told, given my age, they rejected me, because I believe I was 35 years old at the time. They told me and in fact they suggested that if I was willing, I should choose some other unit where they accept volunteers. And the person in the military section mentioned the Serbian Volunteers Guard as a unit I should attempt to join.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you then go to the Serbian Volunteers Guard? Did you enlist?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteers Guard. The place was well-known in Belgrade, because it was Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan's home, across from the Red Star stadium, and I'm one of the team's supporters. Everybody knew about the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did you enlist as a volunteer, and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I enlisted as a volunteer -- I can't remember the date, but I remember it coincided with the fall of Vukovar. I went to the headquarters. That's what the place was called at the time. A few individuals waited for me there. I told them why I was there. It was not really customary for anybody to walk in from the street. For the first couple of days I stayed there, helping to sort out some military equipment. It was in a makeshift garage. We tried to pair shoes and complete uniforms. That was my first encounter with the volunteers and that was my first obligation that I had with them. And after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Excuse me just for a moment. Let me interrupt you. You said that you sorted out some military equipment. Had you served in the military? Could you recognise the military equipment that you were sorting out? Can you describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "military equipment," I mean uniforms and military boots, military footwear. I had served from 1976 to 1978 in Pula. That was a city in Croatia. At that time I served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When it comes to those uniforms and military footwear, did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about them.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Those were conventional olive-drab uniforms and military boots that I remember from the time when I served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How many days did you spend sorting out the equipment, and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I did that for a couple of days, maybe three. And during those two or three days another five or six volunteers arrived. When that job was completed, we were sent to Erdut. First we loaded all the equipment into a van. We ourselves sat in the van and we went to Erdut, to the training centre. That was the place where we were supposed to go. Erdut is some 180 kilometres away from Belgrade in the direction northwards, the Danube, i.e., towards Vukovar. We arrived there and then we were supposed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. When you arrived from Serbia in the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem region, where did you cross the border?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We did it on the so-called Bogojevo bridge. I didn't know it at the time. I learned that only subsequently. On the Serbian side there was the police and the military. The driver was approached by a soldier and I suppose that the driver told him where we were headed. We were not checked at all. We crossed without any problems. From the bridge to the centre of Erdut there is about a kilometre or a kilometre and a half, which means after having travelled that way we arrived at the destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Erdut camp, can you tell us the name of the camp, i.e. -- or rather, tell us first: Who was the first you saw there, at the camp in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at the camp, our first task was to unload the van. Upon our arrival, we changed from our civilian clothes into the uniforms that we ourselves had brought. And then Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, appeared. He came to greet us. At first he shook hands with all of us individually, and then he had a chat with every one of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember what you discussed with Zeljko Raznatovic? What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We just introduced ourselves to each other. I told him who I was and where I was from. And then he asked me about my professional background. I told him what I'd done and what my profession was, and then his comment was, "Thank God that after such a long time finally I have somebody literate in our midst." I don't know how much that meant to me at the time. However, as soon as that short conversation was over, he told me, "You're very welcome, and you will be our clerk." When he said "clerk," he used a somewhat derogatory word, denoting somebody who is an administrative officer. In the military hierarchy, those who served in the JNA will know what that word that he used - and that was the word "cata" - means. I was not really prepared to do that. That was not the reason why I had volunteered. However, that was what he had in mind for me, and that's what I ended up doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, let's now talk about the scope of your work. In performing your duties, did you have a superior? And if that was the case, who was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a superior. I didn't have a supervisor. The only person I had was the commander, Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan. As time went on, our -- he increased my duties, so all of my communication with regard the job was directly with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about your duties. What were your tasks during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Upon my arrival, I started recording the names of the volunteers. And those records had not existed up to then. I maintained the record of the numerical strength, the personal details, and everything that constituted the administration of that unit. In addition to those administrative tasks that I had at the very beginning, my daily duties were to compose daily orders that would be read out every morning as the flag was raised. Those daily orders concerned the training centre of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It was known as the 101st Training Centre. In addition to that, during the course of a day I would have some other regular duties, inter alia, looking after people who had been wounded in combat. When I arrived, there was no combat ongoing, but I found that a certain number of combatants who had been hospitalised around Erdut or in rehabilitation centres. That was a priority, because communications were hindered. When their needs were met, I also had to deal with the logistical issues. The military needed weapons, food, equipment, medicines, toiletries, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's now move on to that part, Mr. Dimitrijevic. When you arrived at the centre, did you come to learn who the centre belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: To be honest, my opinion upon my arrival was completely different; however, with time I realised - or at least that was my impression and it proved to be correct - that we were a very serious organisation that enjoyed the support of all the institutions in the field. When I say that, I mean the Government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem region, as well as the military structures, and I mean the JNA. The centre itself was known as the 101st Centre of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It was in Erdut. It was housed in the barracks of the former recruiting centre of Osijek. It looked, and it still looks, I suppose, as a military facility, and it had everything that I had remembered from the military that I had served in. It had barracks, the cafeteria, the training-grounds, football pitches, training areas, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was training going on in that centre, and who was trained?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The very name of the centre says it all. It was a training centre. Training was going on. And the subject of the training were all the volunteers that had enlisted as the Serbian Volunteer Guard's volunteers. They arrived from Belgrade, they were brought in the same way I had been brought, and they also arrived from all over Slavonia. And they reported at the gate. They were received by the reception service that looked after the volunteers. And then they came to me as individuals. They talked to me. They gave me their name and all the other personal details that were required.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the centre have a military post designation when you arrived or sometime later?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was designated as a military post. I can't remember the exact number, but it did bear the military post designation. That number changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, I would like to call up P500 for your benefit. Could you please look at the document and tell me --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. This is an exhibit under seal, so I would like the Chamber to move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break. And we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, for your information: On the matter raised by Ms. Marcus in relation to disclosure, the Chamber would like to receive an oral response from you tomorrow morning, first thing in the morning. As far as the other matter, that is -- is concerned, that is, the disclosure of documents to be used with future witnesses, the Chamber would like to receive your answer orally not later than Thursday morning or, if time allows, later tomorrow, but we're sitting in the morning. That's the -- these are the time-limits. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, before the break I put a question to you but you didn't have time to answer. From the time that you arrived in the Serbian volunteer unit and performed the duties you performed, from that time onwards or during that period did you ever receive a uniform from the MUP in Serbia or the security service in Serbia? Or if you personally did not receive such uniforms, did you hear anything about such uniforms being delivered to the Serbian voluntary guard unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, was there a weapons warehouse when you arrived in the training centre in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What sort of weapons were there in that warehouse and what sort of weapons were issued to members of the Serbian voluntary guard unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The warehouse had already been set up when I arrived. And when I arrived, it contained automatic rifles, M-70; semi-automatic rifles; hand-grenades; Zoljas; Osas; and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The weapons that you found there -- well, with regard to those weapons, do you know how they were obtained before you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: According to information obtained from members that I met there, I know something about certain cases. And given the duties that I performed, I also found out some information. The first weapons were obtained, to a certain extent, from the JNA. Some of the weapons that the officers had, but not all of them, the Heckler weapons, for example, were treated as war booty. There was one particular event when there was a dispute with the Croats and some Hecklers were found in a warehouse in Zenga and some of the officers had these weapons on them. As for the other weapons that I have already mentioned, they were obtained from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any situations when in the course of action, operations, or training courses ammunition was used and there was the need for new weapons; and if so, how was the situation dealt with?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite natural, because it was a training centre. We had these areas for physical training. We also had a shooting range where the troops were trained and taught how to use those weapons. So ammunition was something that was constantly needed in the course of the training provided. So sometimes we would also need a certain amount of rifles to provide for the warehouse. The volunteers were issued with rifles, and when the volunteers completed their duties they would return the rifle to the warehouse. They would then leave the training centre; someone else would appear and get a weapon. But there were defective weapons as well and some weapons would be lost in operations, so it was necessary for us to remain in constant contact with the JNA, or, rather, with the Territorial Defence, in particular the TO from Western Srijem. We had to remain in constant contact with them in order to provide the warehouse with the relevant supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whom you had contact with in order to obtain supplies for the warehouse, ammunition and weapons for the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We had contact in particular with the Territorial Defence command in Western Srijem. We would list our needs and I personally would take that list to Dalj, which is where I would hand over the list of our needs for that day. And on the following day I was provided with a response in Erdut, but in some cases I directly contacted the army, that is to say the JNA, and requested their assistance if it wasn't possible to obtain assistance in the first place I have mentioned, if it wasn't possible for them to satisfy my needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We have also spoken about obtaining uniforms, and now we are speaking about obtaining weapons. Could you tell us whether you paid for the uniforms and how, if you did, and I have the same question for the ammunition that you tried to obtain.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't pay for any of these things. It wasn't possible for us to pay to anyone because we were members of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia and Baranja, and Western Srijem. So it was also quite logical for me, too, that I shouldn't have to pay for anything. This was quite customary and quite normal for me at the time, and I think that is still the case today. Naturally, as far as the army is concerned, since we were under their command, the Novi Sad Corps was in the field at the time and there were good relationships between our units ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you conclude? Between your unit ...

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Between our unit and the leadership of the corps, or, rather, the JNA, because we participated in these operations together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, you mentioned providing weapons. A little earlier on we spoke about uniforms. You said that you would obtain them from Junk, from someone called Kamenac, a private businessman. Did you pay for those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. We received some donations as the Serbian Volunteer Guards unit, and we used these donations to pay for those uniforms or we would find sponsors who would have direct contact with the producers and would deal with those obligations. So we had absolutely no expenses as far as that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the sponsors who paid for these items were, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of companies who volunteered to be sponsors. There were private businessmen, individuals who would appear with certain funds that they would give, in fact, to the Serbian volunteer guards. There were many private companies, too, that in this way wanted to demonstrate their patriotism. They would give these funds to the Serbian volunteer guards, and there were also some state companies that participated in the entire process. I can give you the names of some of them. The Karic brothers, whatever their company was called, saxin gegoma [phoen], Giovani di Stefano. So these are the individuals that appeared at the time when I was in Erdut for two and a half or three months. Later there were far more individuals or companies of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, you started speaking about the terms you were on with the Novi Sad Corps. At the time that you were in Erdut, at the end of 1991 and 1992, who was the commander of the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: General Biocevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter heard the name correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we verify whether the name was correctly understood by the interpreter. Could you please slowly repeat the name of the commander of the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Giorcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps check on the transcript, Mr. Bakrac, that the name appears --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You have noticed correctly that the first letter in the transcript is G, but it should be B. That's how the witness repeated the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With a B?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then would it then be B-i-o-r-c-e-v-i-c? Would that be the correct spelling? And I left the diacritics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's now have a look at a video extract.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's 2D980. 40 minutes and 37 seconds up until 41 minutes and 21 seconds is the extract we are interested in. It doesn't have a translation. It doesn't have any sound either, Your Honour. I would just like the witness to have a look at the individuals who appear and at the places that we can see in the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, tell us, first of all, with regard to this video, did you manage to recognise the place where this event occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: It's the entrance to the centre, or, rather, this is where the army had its line-up early in the morning. And this individual who appeared and greeted the troops is General Biorcevic, who would go and visit us at the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So if I have understood you correctly, this video extract is an extract of your training centre in Erdut; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did General Biorcevic often go to your centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: One could say so, and that means three or four times a month approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, go to see General Biorcevic; and if so, where did he go to see him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did go to see him frequently. And I could also say that I went to see him frequently. General Biorcevic's command was on a boat on the Danube not far from the centre of Erdut, and I can no longer remember the name of the boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that you went and that Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, went to see General Biorcevic too, can you say what the purpose of your visit was?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I usually went there officially to deal with certain needs that the army would help us with. They'd provide us with some rifles and ammunition and so on and so forth. This relates to your previous questions too. As for Zeljko Raznatovic's visits, I don't know what the purpose was because I wasn't present when he met the general. Sometimes I attended lunches, but these were unofficial occasions. The conversation was unofficial at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any other contact with members of the army, that is to say, of the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I could mention two names, the then-Major Jovanovic and Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Enes Taso. I'm not sure what his rank was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the following document on the screen, D166.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And while waiting for the document to appear on the screen, Mr. Dimitrijevic, tell me, do you know what the relationship was between the Serbian Volunteer Guards and the JNA in the field when it came to engaging in combat and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that there wasn't a single operation at the time -- well, in fact, while I was in Erdut there wasn't much significant activity; but given what I heard and saw and given the documents that I also consulted subsequently, I would say that all the operations were carried out together with the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. There was the command of the Territorial Defence and of the JNA that acted together with the Serbian Volunteer Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, could you have a look at this certificate. This is a certificate dated the 4th of December, 1991. At the time were you in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is a certificate on Markovic Nenad who was seriously wounded. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. His nickname was Sitsko. He lost a leg; it was amputated. His left leg was amputated. He was in hospital in Sombor for a long time, and part of my duties consisted of visiting him almost on a daily basis and of trying to provide for his needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, have you already seen this certificate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I typed it out. I typed this certificate out. And this certificate was typed out to deal with the cost of treating the wounded soldier. There were several such certificates. The procedure was such that I would type out the certificate, Arkan would sign it, it would then be registered, and it would then be taken to the corps command for them to certify. Having certified such a certificate, once the corps command had done that, it was possible to regulate all expenses incurred as a result of the treatment that was required and all expenses incurred for purposes of paying pensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I see a signature in the left-hand corner, Mr. Dimitrijevic. Did you take this to Commander Enes Taso so that he could sign it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Enes Taso didn't sign this, though; somebody signed on his behalf. But I did take it there, and part of my duties consisted of also taking such documents to them to be certified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the basis of this certificate we can see that on the 7th of August, 1991, Nenad Markovic was transferred to the military hospital in Belgrade, which is where his left lower leg was amputated. Could you tell me why it was taken -- why he was taken to the military hospital? And later you were involved in taking care of wounded soldiers. Where were these wounded soldiers from the Serbian Volunteer Guard taken for treatment?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if there were urgent cases in the field and it wasn't possible to transfer a wounded person to that location, then the first medical clinic would be used. All those who could be transported to the military academy would be taken there and they would be treated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know why wounded soldiers from the Serbian Volunteer Guards were taken to the military medical academy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose there was an agreement to that effect at a higher level. There was no way for me to know that. Maybe I can add something to what I've already stated. All the fallen soldiers from various front lines were also transported to the military academy, where a post mortem was carried out. We would then receive their death certificates. And based on those death certificates, we would then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you were involved in all those administrative tasks, what about the pensionable years spent with the Serbian Volunteer Guards, was that recorded in their military booklets?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, certificates had to be issued and those certificates would be taken to the General Staff in Nemanjina Street, and the administrative clerk who was there would stamp the certificates. And then the individuals in question would take those certificates to the relevant institution, where those years would be recorded as pensionable years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's now look at P1189, Mr. Dimitrijevic. This is another certificate signed, seemingly, by the centre commander, Mr. Zeljko Raznatovic. And while we are waiting for the document to appear on the screen, could you please tell us whether the name Ranko Strbac rings a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely what I was talking about. This is a certificate acknowledging that a person was wounded, where the person was treated, how the person was treated, for how long; and based on all that, based on the certificate stamped by the JNA, that individual could claim benefits later on. Some were not even fit to do that, so I would go instead of them. That was also one of my tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that you completed the paperwork for them, what does that mean? Where would you take this certificate before it was sent to the municipal secretariat for health care and social services?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I would take it to the General Staff in Nemanjina Street, the administrative clerk would stamp it, then I would return it to Erdut. And then if the person was from Novi Sad, for example, I would hand it over to him, he would go to Novi Sad, and he would regulate the matters there. If the person was either from Belgrade or elsewhere in Serbia, they would regulate the matters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We don't see the military command stamp. Do you remember if such a certificate was issued in several copies?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of the copies would be kept in the archives of the General Staff, another one in the archives of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, and the individual would receive his own copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question was a bit different. When you issued a certificate, would you keep a copy with the Serbian Volunteer Guards?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One copy would be filed with us, one copy would be given to the individual, and a third copy would be filed at the General Staff, for their records.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, we discussed General Biorcevic's visits to your camp. Did Radovic Stojcevic -- Radovan Stojcevic, Badza, arrive in your camp; and if he did, how often and in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure he arrived. I can't tell you how many times, but I would say that he arrived at least five or six times in a month. Every time when he arrived the troops would be lined up, which meant that his visit was important. His visit was given importance. At that time Radovan Stojcevic, Badza, was the TO commander of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and it was only normal that his visits received such a level of attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember if at any point in time somebody replaced him; and if that was the case, who was it and when was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: In early 1992 Zivorad Trajkovic, whose nickname was Zile Trajkovic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, in your oral testimony you spoke about the relationship with the Novi Sad Corps and about your joint combat activities. Could you please look at a video-clip, 2D976.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I failed to tender 2D980, the previous clip, from 40 minutes, 37 seconds, to 41 seconds -- 41 minutes, 22 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video had been provided without any information about it, but the witness provided a lot of confirming information, therefore we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number for the previous video played by Mr. Bakrac would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number for document 2D980 will be D640, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Jordash, I interpreted your silence as having no objections, and I will continue to do so if you are silent. Then, Mr. Bakrac, the next video.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, 2D976.1. We have a transcript, Your Honour. The transcript has been distributed. It starts at 17.52.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They have laid the mines. I'm sure that they know where they are. They don't know that each of our men can clear the minefields. We want to do that to have everything clear in the morning. In this attack the troops will participate with two makeshift bridges. Two makeshifts bridges will be placed there, tanks will pass and proceed, and we have to carry out a blitz attack. The army promised that they would fire from the tanks on the first houses here. The army will not enter with the tanks. The army has nothing to do there. They are prepared for anti-armoured fight. It is up to us now to do our job."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, we now saw the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the interpreters were not given ample time to find the appropriate transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, we saw Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, providing instructions. Did you recognise the soldiers that were also depicted in the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did recognise some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whom you recognised .

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Ranko Zivanovic, Holma [phoen], Nebojsa Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did they have green helmets and who did you receive the helmets from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did have green helmets on their heads, and we received them from the JNA. We also received some dressings, gas masks. What I'm saying is that we did not receive only ammunition, but, rather, complete sets that included the helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we infer from the video-clip that this is one of the operations that you spoke about as those that were carried out in concert with the military?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can tell that from the clip. I was never present in any of such situations, but this is how things happened and this is what I subsequently heard from the soldiers when they returned to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I tender [Realtime transcript read in error "turn"] the video-clip into evidence, I would like to say that this is a DVD that we received from DFS-009 during the break. And I believe that the Case Manager provided a copy of the DVD to the Prosecutor. I would like to tender the video-clip into evidence. If the Prosecutor needs more time to watch the DVD again, I agree that it should be marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not know the origin until we were just informed just now. Indeed, there's a lot of confusion about the number of videos and the way they were disclosed. So we're not prepared to express our position as to right now, so we agree that it should be MFI'd for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned to the video-clip would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number to be assigned to video-clip 2D976.1 will be D641, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you provide a transcript to the booth before, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I believe that that was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because the booth says that they need some time before you start playing it to find the relevant transcript. Now, you said you received this video during the break, the last break, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. My colleague has provided the booths with several transcripts. I apologise to the booths. Maybe they're not in the right order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is about receiving the video, because I think that -- but let me check in the transcript exactly what you said about that. "... we received -- " you said: "Before I turn" - I take it "tender" - "the video-clip into evidence, I would like to say that this is a DVD that we received from Witness DFS [sic] during the break." Is that during the last break? Or when was that? Or during the recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I meant the winter recess, not the last break in today's sitting. I apologise if I was not clear enough. When I returned to The Hague I made copies of the DVD and I provided one to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was there any reason why you didn't disclose to the Prosecution where you got it from? Because that's what I would have expected you to add as information to the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to be honest, I was busy proofing the witness and I asked my assistant to disclose the DVD to the Prosecutor. It is my mistake that I didn't check how that was done, whether there was an accompanying letter with the DVD; I apologise. My colleague just tells me that there was an accompanying letter, but let me be honest and admit that I never checked that because I was busy proofing this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, when did you receive the video?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This morning or yesterday. This morning or yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, if you received the video during the recess and if you provide it then only yesterday or this morning to Ms. Marcus, of course that could have been done last week easily. I'm not going to spend a lot of time on it, but I look at the matter also in relation to the request by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I arrived last week on Friday or perhaps Thursday. In any case, towards the end of last week. And then I asked my assistant to make copies and then the first working day after the weekend we handed that copy over. And if I was late again, I can only apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Unless you would like to make any further submissions, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in order to save us all time at a later housekeeping session, with respect to this video, I think the information that would be missing from the line of questioning that was asked is -- because Mr. Bakrac asked quite a leading question about inferences that could be drawn from what we see, and the witness said that he had -- was never present in such situations; therefore, although he identified some of the individuals and he made a comment about what they're wearing, he didn't give any information about the timing of the video. And because we don't know any origin information about it, it's -- that's the piece of information I would say right now that is still missing. It's just to give you an opportunity while the witness is here to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is some text in Cyrillic on the video, Ms. Marcus, which may give a clue to the timing. So did --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I see November?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, November 1991. The script is Cyrillic and I believe that the Prosecution has done the same thing. I don't know why the witness shouldn't be allowed to look at the video-clip and tell us whether situations like this were talked about, why he shouldn't be allowed to recognise certain individuals in the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You misunderstood Ms. Marcus. I take it that she didn't say that you're not allowed, but she invited you to seek further clarification, as the timing is concerned, with the witness, if possible; and otherwise, to give clues to the Prosecution as to the timing of the video. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And now can we look at 2D978 from 32 minutes, 27 seconds, to 32 minutes, 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... I think, as a matter of fact, that I may have forgotten to ask for a number to be assigned to the last video or ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is assigned D641, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was marked for identification. Yes, I think I should have -- Ms. Marcus asked for it to be marked for identification and that is what it is now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 2D978, it doesn't have any sound. Could we please have a look at that video-clip. There is no transcript. From 32 minutes and 27 seconds up until 32 minutes and 45 seconds. The video-clip is on the same DVD.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, do you know what is happening in this clip? Can you recognise the situation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you have the tanks that you can see in the clip in mind. This took place around Vukovar. It concerned the fighting around Vukovar. There was a unit from the Serbian Volunteer Guards that captured four tanks that had been so damaged that they couldn't be used. They were immobile. And two tanks were taken from those locations to the centre in Erdut. After the fall of Vukovar, when I arrived in Erdut, I found two tanks there as part of the weapons listed. As we had no tank operators, anyone who had been trained to operate tanks, we gave General Biorcevic those two tanks. I was present there. And he, in return, gave us a certain quantity of weapons that we needed in the warehouse at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you recognise one of those two tanks in this clip?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we mark this document for identification too, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 2D978 will receive number D642, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] D642 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, I asked you who went to the centre, and you answered my question. Now I would like to ask you whether you remember, when you were in the centre, whether there were any official visits to your centre from high UN representatives, from foreign UN representatives?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that was almost on a daily basis. There were visits from the Government of the TO in Baranja and Western Srem and there were their guests as well that went to have conversations with the government in Baranja and Eastern Srijem. The government centre was across the road. I don't know what the name was. So there was just a distance of 5 metres between our doors. And all of the officials who went to visit Western Srijem, Slavonia, and Baranja, and the field, the battle-field, they would be taken by government representatives to visit the centre too. Among them, there were American congressmen as well, senators.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now have a look at 2D979. It's another clip from the same DVD. Item 1. I do apologise. Perhaps it was my mistake. 2D979, item 1, from 36 minute 00 up until 37 minutes 00. Could we just wait a minute. I want to see whether the booths have found the relevant part in the transcript. Yes. So with your leave we can have a look at the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "Arkan hopes his men will eventually form the nucleus of a Serbian army. Many ordinary Serbs are angry with the federal army for signing so many cease-fires, when they'd like to see the war carried further forward into Croat territory. The Serbian opposition has criticised the government for relying too heavily on federal troops, and not forming its own army. Arkan's men could one day have a bigger political role to play. Linda Duffin, Sky News."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "Glad to meet you. "Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic ... Mr. Dimitrijevic, do you remember these visits in November/December 1991 and in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In addition to the individuals I have just seen here, there were many others who visited the centre almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we also mark this video-clip for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our only comment is a question to Mr. Bakrac whether he intends to rely on the words of the narrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would also be my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, it's not my intention to rely on that. It's just that there was that comment. But to be brief: No, it is not my intention to rely on what the journalist said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, was the question to the witness about what was seen in the video? Reference to "these visits," was that a reference to what was seen in the video? Is that ... because I'm trying to understand. We have looked at a video with some comment, then the question asked by you is: "Mr. Dimitrijevic, do you remember these visits ..." Was that a reference to what we had seen on the video? Because we saw a lot of short ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We saw three visits of three high-ranking officials. I asked the witness whether he remembered those visits, and the witness said that in addition to those visits there were many other visits made by high-ranking officials to the centre at the time that he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's then -- I've no problem with the video, but I want to know exactly what -- what it establishes. Did you recognise in each of the small portions that it was a visit and who visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you putting that question to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't receive the interpretation of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, looking at the video, did you recognise all these smaller portions as the visits, the type of visits you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still not. Could Madam Usher -- could we have a -- could we check, first of all that the -- one second, yes, I'm dealing with it. Could we check whether the witness is at the right channel and could we check whether there's any technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. Now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what I -- a question was put to you by Mr. Bakrac. Let me check. He asked you: "... do you remember these visits in November/December 1991 and January 1992 ..." Was -- were these visits the ones you saw in the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I think I arrived after this visit at the centre. This video is a video of three individuals visiting the centre. First there was Owen, Newman, Moody. I think those were the names. I think Owen arrived sometime before I arrived at the centre, and these two gentlemen paid a visit once I had already arrived at the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so for some of the visits you were present during the visits, whereas for other visits you were not but you just conclude on the basis of what you see on your screen that this must have been similar visits as you had been present at. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the three here, yes, I was present for the visit of two of them. But there were far more officials who visited the place. This is just -- here we just have a few visitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, you will understand you had a very simple question: Do you remember these visits? Although, if you put precise questions to the witness, he can't remember them because he wasn't there, for some of them at least. If something is shown to the witness, you should carefully establish what is seen and what the witness himself can tell us about it. Apparently for one of the visits he remembers that that person visited the camp. Could you please be --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I fully accept your criticism. But I'm short of time and I want to get through as much as possible with this witness. I apologise if I do make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that you weren't present when Cyrus Vance visited but you were present for the other two visits. With regard to all three visits, were you able to recognise the place of the visit? Was it -- were these visits, visits to your centre in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all these visits were visits to our centre in Erdut. And these visits took place on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, had we assigned already a number to this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Document 2D979.1 will receive number D643 MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is MFI'd. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Dimitrijevic, was there a press centre next to your centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd like to provide a somewhat detailed explanation if possible. The centre in Erdut is in the actual visit of Erdut next to the wine-producing shop in Erdut which was very popular before the war. That wine-producing shop was taken over by the Government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem -- well, taken over by them, what I mean, in fact, was the building was a solid one, it was well-equipped, and they had the headquarters of the government based in that shop, on those premises, just across the road from the training centre in Erdut. And in front of the building there was another building that was an international press centre for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. And in that press centre that was connected to the Government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem you could find all accredited journalists who were in the area at the time, and they would go to obtain their accreditation from the government. So they were directly across the road. Our centre wasn't walled in, as you could see in the clips. It had a gate, a guard at the gate, but everything else was quite transparent 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In addition to these visits that you have spoken about, were there foreign journalists who also entered your centre to report on it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had such freedom. But they had to announce their arrival in advance. It wasn't possible for anyone to just enter the centre whenever it occurred to them. Volunteers didn't have the right to issue or to give statements of any kind. That was part of the discipline imposed on the Serb Volunteer Guards. Only Zeljko Raznatovic could provide answers to any questions that were put.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We've now spoken about the visits of high-ranking officials. Did anyone from the state security department of Serbia go to visit the training centre, with you being aware of the fact that such an individual was from that centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Not with my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you hear from any members of the SDG that they went to visit the training centre while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember who from the Government or Ministry of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem went to your centre, and how frequently?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the government is concerned, the entire government would visit the centre. Mrgud Milovanovic, for example, Rade Leskovac, some other individuals whose names I have forgotten, but they came on a regular basis, on a daily basis, on a number of occasions, a number of times, in fact. And naturally Goran Hadzic as well, that was obvious. So they would pass through the gate, leave, and this was registered. But they visited the centre quite regularly, on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Goran Hadzic -- or was Goran Hadzic the president of the government at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did he stay in your training centre on occasion? Would he spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a period of time his security was also there. They had some facilities, some premises in the barracks where he would sleep over if he had a lot of duties to perform. I don't know where he lived, but he would come and sleep over. He would eat there. So he was in the training centre itself very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, before I move on to a different topic, can you tell me whether you know anything, and if you do what is it, about the intimate relationships between Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, and the federal security service and Stane Dolanc.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: This is part of an urban myth. An urban myth that could be heard all over the city of Belgrade. After an incident that involved Arkan and some police officers and after -- I'm just speculating, you know. This is not what I know first hand. I'm just sharing stories and rumours with you, that he had something to do with the federal SUP of Yugoslavia, of the republic and the state of Yugoslavia, as it was at the time mand that federal SUP was headed by Mr. Stane Dolanc. But I have nothing to corroborate that. I didn't hear this from him. And if this was to be one of your following questions, I still believe that it was just a myth more than anything else. I don't think that it really did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: However, as far as I understood you, that was a rumour that everybody was familiar with in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The rumour is still being spread. The story is still popular among people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, at one point in time in 1992 you left Erdut and the training centre. Could you tell us when you left and where you went?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: I left in late February or early March 1992. Arkan gave me an order to take over the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guards in Belgrade, in Ljubica Bogdana Street 1. My job description there did not differ much from what I did in Erdut. It was a bit more encompassing. And the main task that I had was to care for the families of the wounded and fallen volunteers. The number two task was to be involved with the procurement to allow the functioning of the guards. I was supposed to obtain materiel that was required. I was also concerned with the well-being of Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan's, family because the headquarters of the volunteers was in his own family home. So those were the main tasks that I was involved with at the headquarters. And one of those tasks was also the reception of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, I moved on to that part in a bit of a haze, but before that I wanted to ask you something about the period where you were still at the training centre in Erdut. You said that you were in charge of procuring food. How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Given the numerical strength at any one time, we were provided by -- food by the Government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. A while ago you asked me about weapons; the same applied to food. I would take the list to Dalj, to the government offices there. They were the ones who provided us with salt, flour, sugar, oil, and such bare necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. While you are talking about that I would like to call up document P1187. This is a document issued in 1992 by the Ministry of Defence of Vukovar. It says here: "We hereby agree that the expenses of the Territorial Defence centre for the training of volunteers in Erdut will be reimbursed to the socially-owned enterprise Dalj," and this document was signed by Mile Milanovic. Was that one of the ways to obtain provisions? Does this approval apply to your centre? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the only way. There was no other centre. When you say the centre in Erdut, that was the 101st Training Centre. Mile Milanovic, who was also known as Mrgud, was a then-minister in the government. He was the one who signed the procurement orders that I would bring to him, and he was the one in charge of paying the invoices. He was the one who made it possible for us to get bare necessities, such as oil, flour, sugar, rice. We also needed toiletries, of course. We needed meat and other such things. I had a vehicle. I had a driver as well. I went on visits to companies in Slavonia and I would present them our needs. I would travel even further afield in Serbia to places such as Apatin, Odzaci, Sombor, all close to Erdut. I would also visit companies there and seek assistance with such provisions. This was all well regulated. People were benevolent towards our requirements and requests. We usually sought toiletries which were in short supply due to war. We never paid for those; however, we reimbursed them by issuing thank-you notes to both individuals and companies that helped us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dimitrijevic. Let's now bring this part to an end, the part which concerns your tour of duty in Erdut. Can you please tell us which vehicles you had in the Erdut centre while you were there.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have a huge fleet of vehicles. We had two Pajero jeeps, small jeeps. We got them from the Vela auto company based in Belgrade, as a gift, as a donation. We had two 5- or 6-passenger vehicles of different makes and different ages. We had two vans, or people-movers; one van for the transportation of goods. That was the one that I most frequently used. We had three lorries, two of which we had obtained from the Army of Yugoslavia. They were nothing much, but they were in a workable order. And we also had a lorry that we had found at the centre. We repaired it and made it workable. In addition to that, the centre also had all the things that I mentioned. We also had a car repair shop, a joinery shop, and we had some people who were very handy and did the repairs themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, at the time when you arrived in late November or early December 1991 until the end of February or beginning of March 1992, while you were there, do you know what registration plates those vehicles had? Did they have registration plates at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Pajeros had Belgrade registration plates because they had arrived from Belgrade. The others didn't have any registration plates, but they were marked with big stickers on the doors and on the bonnet. On the doors the sticker depicted a Serb Volunteer Guards coat of arms which was large enough for everybody to see, and on the bonnet the vehicles were marked by a different type of stickers depicting tigers' heads. This was our moniker; we were known as Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You mentioned two Pajeros with Belgrade registration plates. Were those civilian registration plates or some other plates?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Those were civilian plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The van that you most commonly used, what kind of registration plates did it have?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it had registration plates. This vehicle was registered in Sombor, which is 35 kilometres away from Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what about the other vehicles which did not have any registration plates but, rather, just the stickers, did you ever cross the border to Serbia driving those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How did you move about the area?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The stickers that we had on the doors and on the bonnet were enough for the area. Everybody recognised those vehicles as vehicles belonging to the Serbian volunteers. Nobody else but us had those labels. The van with the Sombor plates that I used, and I say that I used it because that was the logistics -- vehicle for logistics, I didn't have those labels, I just had Sombor registration plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, did the vehicles in question later on receive any registration plates? And if they did, what kind of registration plates were those?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They received registration plates after the Vance Plan was introduced. When the TO was abolished and when we became the Krajina Police, then we received blue registration plates with the marking M for police, without a five-pointed star that had existed before on our registration plates. Instead of that, there was a three-coloured flag and a four-digit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were those registration plates of the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the impression that you suggested that we should have our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are a little bit over the time we usually have, but I was a bit misled by your phrase "let's now bring this part to an end." I thought you would finish that part. Let's take a break. And resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just alert the Court to the fact that Mr. Stanisic had a nose bleed, having taken a pain relief, and may need to leave on a more regular basis for the rest of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- as always, the Chamber respects whatever Mr. Stanisic thinks he needs at that moment. And if this has consequences for the proceedings, we expect you to address us on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if Mr. Stanisic just wants to leave for a second, then that's accepted. But if -- again, if he considers that his right to be present during the proceedings would be -- not be fully respected if we would continue, then of course you would tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Bakrac, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, I would like us to look at a video-clip, 2D977.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check with the booths whether the transcript has been provided. Can we play the video-clip and then I'll have some questions for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We cannot capture all of them. They will all lead to" -- No sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, apparently there is no sound audible for the booth. And even if they have been provided with transcripts, then still they should be able to verify --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether what is found in the transcript is what was said by those appearing on the video. So could you perhaps please do something to put up the volume and perhaps then restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm going to ask the Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I take the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- B/C/S channel, I do not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Bakrac, apparently it's not working. So try to find a solution. And perhaps meanwhile we proceed with other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We'll try and do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, what was the focus of your attention in 1992 when you returned to the headquarters in Belgrade? What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: The first and foremost concern of mine was to look after the wounded and the families of the fallen soldiers. That was the utmost priority. The second-ranking, if I can rank my duties, was the daily receipt of volunteers. The third would be securing financing for Erdut. And in addition to that I also looked after Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan's, family. Their house was next to the headquarters. His wife was there together with their four children. I looked after their safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say that you also secured financing for Erdut, could you tell us where the financing came from, from which funds? Did you fund the headquarters in Belgrade as well as the Erdut requirements?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: There were two or three sources of funding. The first and the most important one was the Simina Mari [phoen] private company that had been incepted. Before Zeljko Raznatovic was the head of the Delije fan club, he had a company that sold the football paraphernalia. And the third source of financing was the bakery that was his property. And later on another company was incepted under the title SDG company. My part of work was to co-ordinate all those companies. The fifth link in that chain were the two shops that belonged to the bakery. And the proceeds of their business also went into the funding of Erdut. Furthermore, we collected and raised money from donors and sponsors. We were heavily involved in PR in order to procure the funds that were needed for certain payments or for helping the families of seriously wounded and fallen soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, while you were in Erdut, and later on, did troops, members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, receive regular salaries?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. That never happened at any time. The volunteers were never paid or compensated in any way for the time that they spent in the Serbian Volunteer Guards unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were any warehouses in Erdut or Belgrade that you had warehouses in which stolen goods from various battle-fields had been left?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: There were no such warehouses. And it wasn't possible to supply such warehouses from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say you gathered funds for the families of killed and wounded soldiers. What sort of form did that assistance take?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly financial aid. But there were other forms of assistance. We'd make it easier for there to be medical treatment for the children of soldiers killed. It would be easier for them to enroll in school. There would be care for them. Provided -- various forms of assistance were provided. Whatever they requested from us was a matter of priority for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, from March 1992 when you returned to Belgrade and onwards, how often did Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, go to the headquarters of the party in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Three or four times a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any circumstances that relate to Mr. Zeljko Raznatovic leaving the Serbian Volunteer Guards to go to the battle-field in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the reasons for that, and I know how they left. At the time I was in Belgrade, and we checked the lists of the volunteers in Belgrade and the situation in Erdut. We did this on a daily basis. So I had to be informed a day earlier that action was being prepared. Or, rather, I was informed of the number of men who were to be involved in that operation, and I took this information into account. The reason for his departure -- well, according to what Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, said, he was a patriot, he was proud of the fact that the president of -- the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had appealed to him to help with the situation in Bijeljina at the time. He was asked to help the Serbs who were under threat there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you something else. You said at the request of a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the name hasn't been recorded. Whose name did you mention?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic, a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, do you know how many SDG combatants went into the field --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the end of counsel's question, as the microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question because you switched off your microphone before you had finished the question, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, Your Honours. I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know how many SDG members went together with Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: Sixty men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know where they left from to go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: They left Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know what the capacity for accommodation was in the camp in the centre in Erdut? And at the beginning of March and at the end of March and beginning of April in Erdut, how many volunteers were there in the centre in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIMITRIJEVIC
utterances.text: As for the accommodation capacity of the Erdut centre, the maximum capacity was 260. During certain periods we had some problems. We had more volunteers than we could receive. And in some cases they were even on waiting lists. So there were never more than 260 individuals in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please now have a look at another video-clip from the collection that the Prosecution disclosed to us. 2D972.1 is the number. One hour, 23 minutes, and 15 seconds is where it starts, up until one hour, 26 minutes, and 59 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
